Results
Constituents of GuHong
Based on literature mining, a total of 163 constituents across seven classes were reported for Honghua (Carthamus tinctorius flowers), that is, 97 flavonoids (including quinochalcones, flavanols, flavones, flavonones, chalcones), nine phenolic acids, 11 organic acids, 12 nucleosides/nucleobase, 25 alkaloids, six spermidines, and three lignans. Articles by Zhou et al.[50], Zhang et al.[51], Xian et al.[52], Yang et al.[53], and Yao et al.[54] provided the most information about Honghua constituents. The information was used to help analyze the composition of GuHong by generating a candidate compound list, which was also used to validate the suitability of the ICP assay for the intended use. As shown in Figure 1, the ICP assay was suitable for composition analysis of GuHong, as indicated by the assay analyte capacity exceeding the required analyte capacity with respect to MW, $\mathrm { L o g } \mathsf { \bar { D } } _ { \mathsf { p H } 7 } , \mathrm { L o g } \mathsf { S } _ { \mathsf { p H } 7 } , \mathrm { H B D } + \mathrm { H B A }$ , and pKa.and nucleobases (61–67), and three spermidines (71–73). Hydroxysafflor yellow A (1; 27.2 μmol/day) was the most abundant Honghua constituent, while guanosine (61), saffloquinoside D (2), uridine (62), 8-hydroxycinnamic acid-8-O-glucoside (51), coumaric acid-4-O-glucoside (52), kaempferol-3-O-rutinoside (21), kaempferol-3- O-sophoroside (22), and chlorogenic acid (53) had lower compound doses (1.0–3.8 μmol/day). N-Acetyl-L-glutamine (81) in GuHong had a compound dose of 3090 μmol/day. GuHong exhibited lot-to-lot variations of 11.3%, 6.9% to 22.3%, 3.3% to 35.4%, and 3% for 1, 61/2/62/51/52/21/22/53, the remaining Honghua constituents, and 81, respectively.Figure 4 shows the human plasma concentration-time profiles of 1, 2, 21, 22, 51, 52, and 53 after intravenous administration of GuHong, and Table 2 summarizes their pharmacokinetic parameters. All these Honghua compounds exhibited small apparent distribution volumes $( V _ { \mathrm { s s } } , 0 . 1 2 – 0 . 4 6 \mathrm { L } / \mathrm { k g } ) ;$ this was due, at least in part, to their poor membrane permeability. The total plasma clearance $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { C L } _ { _ { \mathrm { t o t } , \mathrm { p } } } )$ values of 1 and 2 were significantly lower than that of 52, which were in turn significantly lower than those of 21, 22, 51, and 53. The elimination of 1, 2, and 52 was based on renal excretion, with fractions of doses excreted into urine $( f _ { \mathrm { e - u } } ) _ { \mathit { \Pi } _ { c } }$ ranging from e-u79.4% to 95.6% (mainly via glomerular filtration), and their differences in $\mathrm { C L } _ { \mathrm { t o t , p } }$ appeared to be associated with their unbound fractions in plasma $( f _ { \mathrm { u } } )$ . Unlike these compounds, 21 and 22 were likely eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion (mediated by OATP1B1/1B3 for sinusoidal uptake and MDR1/BCRP/MRP2 for canalicular efflux; Table 3), whereas their renal clearance $( \mathrm { C L } _ { \mathrm { R } } ,$ mediated by tubular secretion via OAT1/2/3) accounted for only 7.9% to 14.4% of the respective excretion of 51 and 53 was also significant $\mathrm { C L } _ { \mathrm { t o t . p } } .$ $( f _ { \mathrm { e - u } } ^ { \mathrm { ~ \tiny ~ 5 4 . 8 \% - } }$ 65.8%) and appeared to involve tubular secretion, which could be mediated by OAT1/2/3 (Table 3). Hepatobiliary excretion, mainly mediated by OATP1B3 for sinusoidal uptake, might also contribute to the elimination of 51 and 53. Owing to the joint differences in $V _ { \mathrm { s s } }$ and $\mathrm { C L } _ { \mathrm { t o t , p } } ,$ 1 had a longer mean elimination half-life $( t _ { 1 / 2 } , 3 . 9$ tot,p hours) than the other Honghua compounds (<1.7 hours); 21 and 22 exhibited very short $t _ { { \scriptscriptstyle 1 } / { \cal 2 } }$ (<5 minutes). No significant accumulation of circulating Honghua compounds occurred during the seven consecutive days of repeated doses of GuHong. No significant sex differences were observed in the human pharmacokinetics of Honghua compounds (Table 2).
